Ofcom published its broadband-speeds consumer guide on 21 November 2022.
The Broadband Speeds Code requires clear speed information when a broadband service is bought.
A signatory provider must allow contract exit without an early-exit fee if an in-network speed problem cannot be fixed within 30 days.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to BT.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to EE.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to NOW Broadband.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to Plusnet.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to Sky.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to TalkTalk.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to Utility Warehouse.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to Virgin Media.
The consumer speed-code protections apply to Zen Internet.
Home-service busy-time speed estimates cover 8pm to 10pm.
Business-service busy-time speed estimates cover noon to 2pm.
A signatory provider should give a minimum guaranteed broadband speed.
For superfast products, minimum-speed information is based on the capability of the line into the premises.
Ofcom recommends an Ethernet-connected computer or tablet for the most accurate speed test because Wi-Fi can slow the signal.
The right to exit can apply to financially, contractually or technically linked bundled products.
The code's 30-day remedy process does not apply to a rolling monthly contract.
Broadband adverts must show the average busy-time speed received by at least 50% of customers.
Ofcom's broadband universal-service consumer page was published on 8 August 2023.
The broadband universal-service consumer page was last updated on 20 March 2026.
Every UK home and business has a legal right to request a decent, affordable broadband connection.
The universal-service definition of decent broadband includes at least 10 Mbit/s download speed.
The universal-service definition of decent broadband includes at least 1 Mbit/s upload speed.
